8.title: what your grandmother was actually doing
8.hook: a flower, a flame, a bell: what's happening at the home shrine
8.howItsDone: At a home shrine, a devotee may offer water, flowers, incense, a waved lamp and food, ring a bell, and then share the food as prasad; temple priests perform puja in the same spirit on a larger scale.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mantra. Your line was a handrail made of sound. When the replay started, did you reach for the rail, even once? Week one is behind you. Week two starts at home. Day eight.

Before the kettle goes on, someone lights a small brass lamp. Beside it: a marigold, fresh this morning, a bell with a handle worn smooth, a stick of incense, a little water in a cup, a sweet on a tiny plate. Some Hindu homes keep a shelf like this, or a corner, or a whole small room, and someone stops there each morning. Walk past it on an ordinary morning and it can look like decoration. Stand and watch for a minute, though, and the person in front of it is busy: pouring, lighting, ringing, setting things down. Their hands are working through something in order. Today's word is the name for what they're doing.
screen: `A LAMP. A FLOWER. A BELL.` → `SOMEONE STOPS THERE EACH MORNING.` → `WHAT ARE THEY DOING?`

segments.voice: Puja. It's usually translated worship, and that's not wrong, but in English the word can sound formal and far away. A home puja is close and small, and it's done with the hands. Watch the steps. Water is offered. A flower is set down. Incense is lit. A lamp is waved. A bell is rung. Food is offered, and afterward it comes back as prasad, a gift to be eaten. Families and regions do it differently, and some teachers describe the whole thing as welcoming God as an honored guest. Now listen to the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna, speaking as God, says that whoever offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, with devotion, he accepts it. In Sanskrit it begins: patram pushpam phalam toyam. A leaf. A flower. A fruit. Water. Nothing on that list costs much. What the verse cares about is the devotion, the heart that comes with the gift. So here's one way in, for anyone, whatever they believe. Puja gives a person's attention one place to land, and walks it through one sense after another: the cool of the water, the color of the flower, the smell of the smoke, the sound of the bell, the taste of the sweet. For those few minutes, the whole person is in one place. Maybe that's why the shrine can be so simple: a picture, a small stone, a lamp. The size of the offering was never the point. The care is. Seen that way, a grandmother at that shelf every morning isn't only keeping a custom. She's spending her attention on purpose, before anything else can claim it.
screen: `WATER, FLOWER, FLAME, BELL, FOOD` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER` · `ONE SENSE AFTER ANOTHER` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one ordinary thing. No shelf needed. Look around and choose one object you can see: a cup, a plant, your own open hand. Give it your eyes first, its color and its edges. Then, if you can reach it, your touch. Then close your eyes and keep the picture of it. If you pray, you can offer this small attention to God. If you don't, just let one thing have all of you for a little while. The bell holds the time.
Puja. Honor, offered with the hands and the senses: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water. Eighth word.
Your line: attention is an offering. Today, give one ordinary thing your whole attention: a meal, a face, a cup of tea. One minute, nothing else in your hands. Day eight.

9.title: not fate, not payback
9.hook: the word everyone borrows, and what it actually says
9.howItsDone: Hindu teachers speak of karma as action and its fruit, within this life and across lifetimes; schools of thought differ on how karma works and on how a person is freed from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: puja. Your line was attention is an offering. What got your whole attention, even for a minute? Today's word gets borrowed a lot. Day nine.

Karma. Someone says it when the car that cut them off gets stopped at the next light. Someone says it when a person who was unkind finally has a bad week. It turns up in song lyrics, on coffee mugs, under photos. Used like that, it means payback: the universe keeping a ledger and settling it on schedule, ideally where you can watch. It's a satisfying idea. It is also not quite what the word means. The older meaning is less about getting even and more about getting made, and it turns the whole thing around to face the one who's using it.
screen: `KARMA.` → `THE CAR AT THE RED LIGHT.` → `PAYBACK?` → `NOT QUITE.`

segments.voice: Karma is the Sanskrit word for action. A deed. Work. Something done. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna points out that no one can stay without acting, even for a moment. Breathing, eating, speaking, choosing: all of it is action. So the first thing to know is that karma isn't something that happens to you. It's what you do. The second thing is what action does back. One of the old Upanishads, the Brihadaranyaka, says it in a line that sounds almost like a proverb: yathakari yathachari tatha bhavati. As a person acts, as a person behaves, so that person becomes. Not: so the person is punished. Becomes. Patience, practiced, turns into a patient person. Sharpness, practiced, turns into a sharp one. A mango seed isn't judged worthy of a mango tree; it grows one because that's what the seed is. Here's why that matters on an ordinary afternoon. The payback version keeps your eyes on other people: did they get what's coming? The older version turns you around: what am I growing, right now, with this next word? The other driver's action is theirs. What you do in the next few seconds is yours. The same Upanishad passage goes on to speak of what happens after death, and Hindu teachers speak of karma across lifetimes too, the actions of one life shaping the next. Schools differ on how that works, and on how a person is finally freed from it. For today, stay with the line in that old text: as you act, so you become.
screen: `KARMA — ACTION, A DEED` · `NO ONE STAYS WITHOUT ACTING` · `AS ONE ACTS, SO ONE BECOMES` · `ACROSS LIFETIMES, TOO` · then, large: `WHAT YOU DO, YOU BECOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one seed. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small thing you did this week: a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or skipped. Don't grade it. Just ask what it's growing. A habit? A mood in the room? A way you're becoming? Then choose one action you'd be glad to see grow, and hold it in mind. Some people offer an action to God before doing it; that's one way to hold it too. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, and what action makes of the one who does it. Not payback. Ninth word.
Your line: what you do, you become. Today, choose one small action you'd be glad to have grow, and do it on purpose. Day nine.

10.title: the one behind your eyes
10.hook: what stays when everything else about you changes
10.tomorrow: the ocean the wave forgets it is
10.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Upanishads study the self through teachers and texts, and in meditation and self-inquiry turn attention from thoughts to the one who is aware of them; schools differ on how the self relates to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma. Your line was what you do, you become. Did you plant one thing on purpose? Today we turn from what gets done to the one doing it. Day ten.

A question with no trick in it. Who is hearing this sentence? Not what. Who. The quick answer is: me. But try pointing at the me. The body? It has been changing since childhood. The mood? It may have shifted twice since breakfast. The thoughts? They're moving faster than this voice. Everything you can point to keeps moving. And yet, the Upanishads say, something has been there for all of it, the one all of it happened to. A teacher in an old Hindu text was pressed on exactly this, and his answer turned the question around. Today's word is what he was pointing at.
screen: `WHO IS HEARING THIS?` → `NOT THE BODY. NOT THE MOOD.` → `SOMETHING HAS BEEN THERE FOR ALL OF IT.`

segments.voice: Atman. The self. Not the self in selfie, the personality you show the world. The Upanishads use atman for the deepest you: the one that is aware. And they notice something strange about it. You can't look straight at it. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, a questioner keeps pressing the teacher Yajnavalkya: show me this self, plainly, the way you'd point and say, that's a cow, that's a horse. And Yajnavalkya answers, in effect: you can't see the seer of seeing. You can't hear the hearer of hearing. The one who looks can't become one more thing on the table to be looked at. So, in other passages, the same Upanishad describes the self by saying what it is not: neti, neti. Not this, not this. Whatever you can point to, the body, the breath, the busy mind, the self is not that. One way to put the Upanishad's point: take away everything that can be watched, and what's left is the watching. Put plainly: someone is in there. Today that someone gets its name. Here's where it turns practical. When worry comes, it comes as something seen: a thought, a tight chest, a story about tomorrow. The Upanishad points past it, to the one who sees. Hindu schools describe the atman in different ways. Some teach that the self is one with the whole. Others teach that it is a distinct soul, forever dear to God and dependent on God. Tomorrow brings the word for the whole. Today, just the turn this word makes: away from what's being watched, toward the one who is watching.
screen: `ATMAN — THE SELF THAT IS AWARE` · `THE SEER OF SEEING` · `NETI, NETI — NOT THIS, NOT THIS` · `THE WATCHING, NOT THE WATCHED` · then, large: `SOMEONE IS IN THERE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice the noticer. Let your eyes close or soften. Let a thought arrive, any thought. Don't follow it. Just see that it's there. Now notice that something saw it. Rest there for a moment, not in the thought, in the seeing. Another thought will come; that's what thoughts do. Same move: see it, then notice the one who saw. No need to get anywhere. The bell holds the time.
Atman. The self: not the body, not the thoughts, but the one aware of them. Tenth word.
Your line: someone is in there. When worry shows up today, ask once, quietly: who is seeing this? Just the question. Day ten.

11.title: the ocean the wave forgets it is
11.hook: salt in a cup of water, and rivers that reach the sea
11.tomorrow: anyone who turns a light on
11.howItsDone: Hindus study the Upanishads' teaching on Brahman with teachers and commentaries, and the schools of Vedanta (Shankara's Advaita, Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, Madhva's Dvaita) each read 'tat tvam asi' in their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atman, the one behind your eyes. Your line was someone is in there. Did you catch yourself watching a thought? Today the word gets bigger, so we'll go slow. Day eleven.

A father hands his son a lump of salt and says: put this in a cup of water, and come back in the morning. The son does. Next morning the father says: bring me the salt. The boy looks. It's gone. Sip from the top, says the father. Salty. From the middle. Salty. From the bottom. Salty. The salt is in every sip, and he can't find it anywhere. The father is Uddalaka, the son is Shvetaketu, and the story is told in the Chandogya Upanishad. It's one of the old ways of pointing at today's word, and the word is a big one.
screen: `A LUMP OF SALT. A CUP OF WATER.` → `WHERE DID IT GO?` → `IT'S IN EVERY SIP.`

segments.voice: Brahman. Not Brahma, the creator god in the stories, and not Brahmin, the priestly class. Different words. Brahman is the name the Upanishads give to the whole: the reality underneath everything, what everything comes from and returns to. Like the salt, it isn't one more thing you can pick out. It's in every taste. The same chapter of the Chandogya has another picture. Rivers flow, some east, some west, and in the end they reach the sea and become the sea. And once there, the Upanishad says, they don't know: I am this river, I am that one. Now the line the father keeps saying to his son, again and again in that chapter: tat tvam asi. That's what you are. Yesterday's word, atman, the self, and today's word, Brahman, the whole: the Upanishad brings them face to face. Hindu thinkers read the line in more than one way. Advaita Vedanta, taught by Shankara, reads it as identity: the self and the whole are not two. Ramanuja's school reads it as one whole with real differences inside it, the self living in God and God as the self's inner ruler. Madhva's school keeps the self and God distinct, the self always dependent on God. These readings sit side by side in the tradition, and nobody here has to choose. Just notice what the picture does. In the Upanishad, the rivers don't dry up somewhere along the way. They become the sea. And today's title borrows the picture for one way of hearing it: a wave that is ocean the whole time, even while it forgets.
screen: `BRAHMAN — THE WHOLE` · `SALT IN WATER, RIVERS IN THE SEA` · `TAT TVAM ASI — THAT'S WHAT YOU ARE` · `READ MORE THAN ONE WAY` · then, large: `NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the river reach the sea. Sit and breathe. Bring a river to mind, any one you've seen or can imagine. Let it carry this life, this name, today's worries. Follow it as it moves. Then let it reach the sea, and let the edges go. Not lost: arrived. Rest there, in the big water. Some rest there with one name of God in mind. The bell holds the time.
Brahman. The whole, the reality under everything. Not Brahma, not Brahmin. Eleventh word.
Your line: not two. When you feel cut off from someone today, try the rivers and the sea for one breath. Day eleven.

12.title: anyone who turns a light on
12.hook: the word got borrowed for salesmen; the old meaning is closer to a lamp
12.howItsDone: Hindus may learn from a guru within a lineage (parampara), receive instruction or a mantra from them, and honor teachers on Guru Purnima; in some traditions, God is understood as the first or inner guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Brahman. Your line was not two. If it felt too big, that's all right; it's a word to grow into. Today is smaller and closer to home. Day twelve.

Marketing guru. Fitness guru. Some guru with an online course and a very confident voice. In everyday English the word has drifted toward a person with something to sell. In Hindu tradition it names something far more personal, and the thing it describes may already be in your life without the word ever being used. A grandparent at the kitchen table. A coach. A teacher who stayed after class. A friend who said one true sentence at exactly the right time. Today's word is for that person.
screen: `MARKETING GURU. FITNESS GURU.` → `THE OLDER MEANING.` → `ONE TRUE SENTENCE, AT THE RIGHT TIME.`

segments.voice: Guru. A teacher, but in this tradition more than a teacher of facts. A guru is someone who helps you see. An Upanishad called the Advaya Taraka plays with the sound of the word: the syllable gu, it says, means darkness, and ru is what stops it. Wordplay, not a dictionary entry, but a vivid one. A guru is the one who removes the dark. Yesterday you met one without the title. Uddalaka, with the cup of salt water, was a father acting as a guru, teaching his son by letting him taste. In stories like that one, learning happens up close, in a relationship, one person to another. The Mundaka Upanishad says that someone who wants to know should go to a teacher with fuel in hand, firewood for the teacher's fire, a small gift and a sign of willingness to serve. And the teacher, it says, should be learned in the texts and steady in Brahman. Two things there. The student comes humbly. The teacher has to be the real thing. Hindu traditions honor gurus in more than one way. Some follow one teacher for life, inside a long line of teachers. For some, God is the first guru, or the guru within. And on Guru Purnima, a full-moon festival, students thank their teachers. But keep the Advaya Taraka's picture close: someone stood where you were stuck, and the dark lifted. Today's title says it: anyone who turns a light on. A guru isn't only a job title. It can be a moment.
screen: `GU — DARKNESS, RU — WHAT STOPS IT` · `A FATHER WITH A CUP OF SALT WATER` · `GO WITH FUEL IN HAND` · `A MOMENT, NOT JUST A TITLE` · then, large: `ANYONE WHO TURNS A LIGHT ON.`

segments.voice: Today, remember one light. Rest your hands in your lap. Bring to mind one time someone helped you see. One sentence, one afternoon, one look. Let their face come. Hear it again, if you can. Then, silently, thank them. If you pray, you can thank God for them too. Sit for a moment in what the room looked like once the light was on. The bell holds the time.
Guru. A teacher who helps you see; in one Upanishad's play on the sound, the one who removes the dark. Twelfth word.
Your line: thank a teacher today. The actual person, if you can reach them. Two lines in a message are plenty. Day twelve.

13.title: why 108
13.hook: beads moving through someone's fingers, and the number on the string
13.carry: count what you want to keep
13.howItsDone: Devotees do japa with a mala, moving one bead per repetition of a mantra or a divine name, often at a set time each day; some count on the sections of the fingers instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: guru. Your line was thank a teacher today. Did a name come to mind? Today the handrail gets a counter. Day thirteen.

Ask why a mala has a hundred and eight beads and you may hear a different answer each time. Watch one in use first. Beads move through someone's fingers, one at a time: wooden beads, or seeds, or stones, on a string, with one larger bead at the top that, by custom, the fingers don't pass over. The lips move without sound. The thumb draws the next bead forward. By tradition, a full Hindu mala carries a hundred and eight beads, plus that one at the top. The number can wait. A better question comes first: what is the person with the beads actually doing?
screen: `BEADS ON A STRING.` → `LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` → `WHY 108?`

segments.voice: Japa. Repeating a mantra, or a name of God, again and again, often counted. On day seven, the mantra was a handrail made of sound. Japa is walking the whole staircase with your hand on it. The beads are the counter: one bead, one repetition. The hand keeps count so the mind doesn't have to, and the mind is free to stay with the sound. Back then you heard that the Bhagavad Gita names japa among offerings. Here is the verse around it. In the tenth chapter, Krishna names where he can be found. Among things that don't move, the Himalaya. Among words, the one syllable, om. And among offerings, he says, I am the offering of japa. The Sanskrit is yajnanam japa-yajno 'smi. Of all the ways to make an offering, here is one that needs no fire and no flowers. Just a name, said again. Now, why a hundred and eight? People give answers from the sky, from lists of divine names, from the body. None of them comes from a text this lesson can put in front of you, so we'll leave the question open, honestly. But there's something simpler worth noticing about any fixed count. It gives the practice an end. You know when you're done. You don't have to decide, halfway through, whether you've done enough; the string decides. And a practice that can be finished today can be picked up again tomorrow, and the day after. That's how a practice gets kept. So the number on the string may hold mysteries, but it also does a plain job: it turns a good intention into something you can count.
screen: `JAPA — A NAME, SAID AGAIN` · `THE HAND COUNTS, THE MIND RESTS` · `I AM JAPA, AMONG OFFERINGS` · `A FIXED COUNT GIVES AN END` · then, large: `COUNT WHAT YOU WANT TO KEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count on your fingers. No beads needed. Each finger has three sections. Touch your thumb to the top section of your index finger: one. The middle section: two. The base: three. Then on to the next finger. With each touch, say om silently on the out-breath, or, if you pray, a name of God you use. Go slowly. You won't reach a hundred and eight today, and you don't need to. The bell holds the time.
Japa. Repeating a mantra or a name, counted, so the hand keeps count and the mind can rest. Thirteenth word.
Your line: count what you want to keep. Once today, under a desk or on a train, count a few quiet oms on your fingers. Nobody will know. Day thirteen.

14.title: light passed hand to hand
14.hook: a flame on a plate, moved in circles, then carried around the room
14.howItsDone: Arti is performed in temples and homes, often in the morning and evening: a lamp is waved before the image of God while a bell rings and a song is sung, and then the flame is brought to each person, who passes their hands over it and touches their eyes and forehead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: japa. Your line was count what you want to keep. Did you count a few on your fingers? Two weeks today. Day fourteen.

segments.voice: Evening at a temple. Or the steps down to a river, as dusk comes in. Or a living room, when the lamp comes out. A small flame sits on a metal plate, and someone moves it in slow circles in front of the shrine. A bell rings. People sing. Then the plate is carried around the room, and one by one, people pass their hands over the flame and bring their palms to their eyes and forehead. It takes a few minutes, start to finish. Today's word is that flame, and what happens when it leaves the shrine.
screen: `A FLAME ON A PLATE.` → `SLOW CIRCLES. A BELL.` → `THEN IT COMES TO THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Arti. The waving of a lamp; the offering of light. It often closes a puja, the word from day eight: after the water and flowers and food, the lamp is circled before the image of God, and a song is sung. One arti song begins: Om jai jagadish hare. Victory to you, lord of the world. There's a line in the Katha Upanishad that helps with what the lamp might mean. The sun doesn't shine there, it says, nor the moon and stars, nor lightning, let alone this little fire. Then: tam eva bhantam anubhati sarvam. Everything shines after that one shining; by its light all this is lit. So when a small flame is held up before God, some teachers read it as light offered back to where light comes from. It's a humble gift. The lamp knows where its shine came from. Then the flame leaves the shrine and goes out to the people. Each person draws its warmth toward their face, taking some of the blessing in. The same small fire touches every face in the room. Nobody gets more of it. Nobody needs to. That's the picture in today's line: light passed hand to hand. That may be part of the pull of the evening arti. The day is going dark, and people make a small light on purpose, together, and share it.
screen: `ARTI — THE OFFERING OF LIGHT` · `EVERYTHING SHINES AFTER THAT ONE` · `LIGHT OFFERED BACK TO ITS SOURCE` · `THE SAME FIRE TOUCHES EVERY FACE` · then, large: `LIGHT PASSED HAND TO HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the light, and pass it on. If there's a candle or a lamp near you, light it; if not, any light in the room will do. Look at it for a breath. Then cup your hands toward it, as if gathering warmth, and bring them to your eyes and forehead. Now bring one person to mind, near or far, and turn your cupped hands toward them, as if passing the plate. Then sit with the light. The bell holds the time.
Arti. The offering of light, and then the light shared with everyone. Fourteenth word. Puja, karma, atman, Brahman, guru, japa, arti: that's week two.
Your line: light passed hand to hand. Tonight, as it gets dark: one small light, one breath, one person you send it to. Next week brings the doing words. Day fourteen.
